## Declarations and implementations

```plato
//==
// # Finite elements
//
// The vocabulary of a linear-elastic finite-element analysis
// (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_element_method): what an analysis is
// posed over, how it is restrained and loaded, what a solve returns, and how the
// answer is read back. The bodies are in `finite-elements.library.plato`; the
// material record and the beam the 1D path analyses are in
// `engineering.types.plato`.
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - Element formulation
//  - Degrees of freedom, supports and loads
//  - Continuum models
//  - The linear system and its solution
//  - Analysis results

//==
// # Element formulation
//
// Which two-dimensional idealization a plate element stands for. The
// three-dimensional constitutive constants themselves are `LameParameters`
// (`engineering.types.plato`), which both idealizations reduce to.

// Which out-of-plane assumption a two-dimensional element makes: a thin sheet
// free to contract through its thickness so that the out-of-plane stress is
// zero (PlaneStress), or a slice of a long body held against contracting so
// that the out-of-plane STRAIN is zero (PlaneStrain).
// (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_stress)
type PlaneCondition = PlaneStress | PlaneStrain;

//==
// # Degrees of freedom, supports and loads
//
// A degree of freedom is one scalar unknown of the assembled system. Every model
// here numbers them the same way: node n's component r is degree of freedom
// n * D + r, where D is the number of components a node carries — three for a
// solid, two for a plane element, two (deflection then rotation) for a beam.
// That one rule is what lets the element kernels, the assembler and the solver
// below stay independent of each other.

// A zero-based index of one scalar unknown of the assembled system ("degree of
// freedom"). -1 means "none".
// Convention: see CONVENTIONS.md - Typed indices.
type DofIndex
    implements IValue, IHashable, IComparable, IIndex
{
    Value: Integer;
}

// One degree of freedom held at a known value — the essential (Dirichlet)
// boundary condition. Displacement is in that degree of freedom's own unit:
// meters for a translation, radians for a beam rotation. A support that
// restrains a node without moving it is this record with a zero value; a
// prescribed settlement or a stretched fixture is the same record with a
// non-zero one.
// (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_boundary_condition)
type PrescribedDisplacement
    implements IValue
{
    Dof: DofIndex;
    Displacement: Number;
}

// One contribution to the load vector: a degree of freedom and the amount added
// to it, in newtons for a translation and newton-meters for a beam rotation.
//
// Every load in this vocabulary is resolved into a list of these before anything
// is summed, which keeps "which degrees of freedom does this load reach, and in
// what proportion" — the part that differs per load type and per element — apart
// from the accumulation, which is one shared function. Contributions may repeat
// a degree of freedom; they add.
type DofLoad
    implements IValue
{
    Dof: DofIndex;
    Amount: Number;
}

// A concentrated force applied at one node of a solid model, in newtons.
type NodalForce3D
    implements IValue
{
    Node: VertexIndex;
    Force: Vector3D;
}

// A concentrated force applied at one node of a plane model, in newtons. The
// force is the total on the modelled thickness, not a force per unit thickness.
type NodalForce2D
    implements IValue
{
    Node: VertexIndex;
    Force: Vector2D;
}

// A uniform surface traction over one boundary triangle of a solid model, in
// pascals. The traction vector is the force per unit area, in world axes, so a
// pressure is the inward face normal scaled by its magnitude.
// (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traction_(engineering))
type FaceTraction3D
    implements IValue
{
    Face: TriangleFace;
    Traction: Vector3D;
}

//==
// # Continuum models
//
// An analysis posed over a mesh: the geometry, one isotropic material, and the
// restraints and loads. Both models carry Gravity as an ACCELERATION rather than
// as a force, so the body force follows from the material density and the
// element measure and does not have to be lumped by the caller; a zero vector
// means no body force.

// A linear-elastic analysis of a solid meshed into constant-strain tetrahedra.
// Tractions act on triangles whose vertex indices name Mesh.Positions; they are
// not checked against the mesh boundary, so a face in the interior is a modelling
// error rather than a detected one.
// (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_element_method)
type ElasticModel3D
{
    Mesh: TetrahedralMesh3D;
    Material: EngineeringMaterial;
    Constraints: Array<PrescribedDisplacement>;
    Forces: Array<NodalForce3D>;
    Tractions: Array<FaceTraction3D>;
    Gravity: Vector3D;
}

// A linear-elastic analysis of a plate meshed into constant-strain triangles,
// under one of the two plane idealizations. Thickness is uniform and is the
// out-of-plane extent the element measure multiplies by.
// (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_stress)
type ElasticModel2D
{
    Mesh: TriangleMesh2D;
    Material: EngineeringMaterial;
    Thickness: Length;
    Condition: PlaneCondition;
    Constraints: Array<PrescribedDisplacement>;
    Forces: Array<NodalForce2D>;
    Gravity: Vector2D;
}
```
